rationale: CRC-associated oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella and similar genera) each show up in only a few samples and at low abundance. That makes them weak as separate random-forest split variables. So I'm adding two aggregate features: the log of their combined relative abundance, and the number of marker genera detected. Together these give the forest one strong, denser signal, and because they are built from taxonomy names they should carry over to the external studies.

Baxter's main CRC signal is a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) that tend to show up together in tumors, but each one is sparse and missing from most samples. To let the random forest use that combined signal in a single split, I add two composite features built from taxonomy names: the log of their summed relative abundance, and how many of the five are detected above 1e-4. Because they rely on taxonomy names only, they should also carry over to the external CRC studies.

CRC's best-replicated stool signal is a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas/Micromonas, Peptostreptococcus, Gemella). Each is sparse and appears in only a few patients, so a random forest picking ~16 random genera per split often misses them. This change adds two summary features built from taxonomy names, so they also work on the other studies: the log of the group's combined abundance, and how many of the five are present.

CRC cases in Baxter carry a sparse, patchy set of oral pathobionts: Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas and Gemella. Any one tumour usually has only some of them, so each genus alone splits poorly in a random forest. I'm adding two features that pool these taxa: their summed log relative abundance and the number of them detected (presence above a small threshold). The forest can then catch cases with any member of the group in one split. The features are built from taxonomy names, so they should also carry over to the external CRC studies.

I'm adding two marker features built from the known CRC oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas): their combined log relative abundance and how many of them are present. In Baxter 2016 these genera are the strongest CRC signals, but they are rare and sparse. Spread over about 200 genus columns, the random forest seldom picks them at a split, so a single summary feature should make the signal easier to use. Because the features are matched by taxonomy name rather than study-specific OTU ids, they should also carry over to the four external CRC studies. This hasn't been run yet, so I don't have a Dev score for it.

CRC is strongly linked to a small group of oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas, Gemella) that tend to appear together in tumours. Each one is rare and sparse, so the random forest has to combine many weak single-genus splits to use them. This change adds two summary features built from genus names: the summed log abundance of these markers and how many of them are detected. Because they use taxonomy names, not study-specific OTU ids, they should also carry over to the external CRC studies.

I'm adding two features built from the four oral pathogens most consistently linked to CRC (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas): their summed relative abundance on a log scale, and how many of the four are detected. Each one is rare and patchy, so the random forest rarely splits on them one at a time; a pooled score should give a stronger signal. It is also defined by taxonomy names, so it should carry over to the external CRC studies.

CRC stool signal comes mostly from a small group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and shows up in only some patients, so the random forest rarely picks any single genus. I'm adding one combined oral-pathogen abundance feature and a count of how many of these markers are detected. Both use taxonomy names, so they should carry over to the four external studies.

CRC-enriched oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas/Micromonas, Porphyromonas, Gemella) are each sparse, so the random forest rarely uses them individually. I'm adding aggregate marker features built from genus names: the summed abundance, its log, and how many marker genera are detected. Because they use taxonomy names rather than OTU ids, they give the forest one strong, dense signal that should also carry over to the external studies.

CRC-enriched oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) are each present in only a few samples, so a random forest on separate genera spreads their signal thinly across rare features. This change adds a combined, taxonomy-name-based score: the log of their summed relative abundance plus a count of how many are detected. It should help on this study and carry over to the external CRC studies.

CRC-enriched oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas, Gemella) are each rare and only sometimes detected, so one random-forest split on any single genus catches few cases. Because these genera tend to appear together in tumour-associated stool, I'm adding two pooled features: the log of their summed relative abundance and the number of these genera detected. This gives the forest a denser signal it can split on, and since it uses taxonomy names rather than study-specific OTU ids it should carry over to the four external CRC studies.

Baxter 2016 found that the CRC signal comes mostly from a group of oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas). Each one is rare and patchy, so a random forest has trouble combining them through separate splits. I'm adding two pooled features: total oral-pathogen relative abundance and the number of these genera present. Both use taxonomy names only, so they should carry over to the external studies.

The known CRC markers are oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and low in abundance, so a random forest only picks up their signal weakly. This change adds two label-free summary features: the log of their combined relative abundance and the number of them detected per sample. These should be stronger, depth-robust biomarkers that rely only on genus names, so they also carry over to the external CRC studies.

Baxter et al. found that the CRC signal in stool is mostly a small group of oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and only weakly informative alone, so I'm adding two features that combine them: the log of their summed abundance and how many of them are detected. The random forest can then split on the combined signal directly instead of piecing it together from noisy individual columns. The features use taxonomy names, not study-specific OTU ids, so they should carry over to the four external CRC studies.

Across CRC cohorts, the most consistent signal is a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) that turn up together in tumour-associated stool. Each one is rare and sparse, so a random forest has trouble splitting on them one at a time. I'm adding two label-free features matched by taxonomy name: the summed relative abundance of these genera and how many of them are present. Because they use names rather than study-specific OTU ids, they should also carry over to the external studies.

CRC's strongest stool signal is a group of oral pathogens that tend to occur together (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and low in abundance, so the RF's random feature subsets rarely catch them as single genera. This change adds explicit features built from genus names (summed log abundance, a count of how many are present, and a log-ratio of pathogens to butyrate producers), so the model can use the combined signal, and because the features rely on names rather than study-specific OTU ids they should carry over to the external studies.

CRC samples consistently carry several oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas), each one sparse and low in abundance. A random forest has a hard time combining them from separate splits. This change adds two features: their summed relative abundance and the number of these genera detected in a sample. Both are built from taxonomy names, so the same features should carry over to the external CRC studies.

CRC's best-replicated signal is a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and present in only some patients, so a random forest splitting on single genera uses them poorly. This change adds two features: the log of their combined relative abundance, and a count of how many are present above 1e-4. Both are built from genus names, not study-specific OTU ids, so they should carry over to the four external CRC studies.

Baxter 2016 and later CRC meta-analyses found that the most consistent stool signal of CRC is a small group of oral-pathogen genera: Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus and Gemella. Each one is rare and sparse, so a random forest on ~200 relative-abundance genera struggles to use them. I'm adding two summary features built from their genus names: a summed log-abundance score and a count of how many marker genera are present. Because they use taxonomy names rather than study-specific OTU ids, they should also carry over to the four external CRC studies.

CRC-associated oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) are each sparse and found in only some patients, so a random forest that splits on one genus at a time catches each signal only weakly. I'm adding a combined "oral-pathogen load" score (log of summed relative abundance and the number of marker genera present). These are matched by taxonomy name, so the features carry over to the external CRC studies.
